nameStory: This plant earned the charming name 'lamb's-ear' because its incredibly soft, fuzzy leaves feel exactly like touching a lamb's velvety ear! The scientific name 'byzantina' refers to the Byzantine Empire region where it originates, while 'woolly hedgenettle' describes both its fuzzy texture and its membership in the nettle family.
description: Woolly hedgenettle is a low-growing perennial herb that forms soft, silvery-gray carpets in gardens and occasionally escapes to naturalize in the wild. The plant stays close to the ground most of the year, with thick, oval leaves covered in dense, woolly hairs that give it an almost fake, plush appearance. In late spring and early summer, it sends up tall flowering spikes that can reach 1-3 feet high, topped with small purple flowers. This Middle Eastern native is primarily grown as an ornamental but occasionally pops up in unexpected places as a garden escapee.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, oval leaves covered in incredibly dense, soft white hairs that feel like velvet or lamb's wool - you'll want to keep touching them! The silvery-gray appearance is unmistakable.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, light purple flowers arranged in whorls around tall, upright spikes that rise well above the leafy base in late spring and early summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats of foliage that hug the ground, with dramatic vertical flower spikes shooting up when blooming.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems typical of the mint family, also covered in the same woolly white hairs as the leaves.

habitat: In New England, woolly hedgenettle is most commonly found as a garden escapee near homes, old foundations, and disturbed areas where it has spread from ornamental plantings. It prefers well-drained soils and sunny to partially shaded locations, often appearing along roadsides, field edges, and waste areas. The 22 observations in New England suggest it's still relatively uncommon in the wild here.

seasonality.spring: New silvery-gray leaves emerge from overwintered crowns, quickly forming the characteristic woolly carpet. Tall flower spikes begin developing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with purple flower spikes at full height. The woolly leaves remain prominent and easily identifiable throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes dry and turn brown while the woolly basal leaves often remain green, preparing to overwinter in mild areas.
seasonality.winter: In harsh New England winters, above-ground parts may die back completely, but the plant often survives and regrows from underground crowns in spring.

funFact: The leaves are so absorbent and soft that they were traditionally used as natural bandages and toilet paper - the plant was literally nature's tissue box!
confusionNotes: The incredibly soft, woolly texture makes this plant nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England - no native plant has leaves that feel quite this much like fabric or fur.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hedgenettle,' this plant doesn't sting at all - quite the opposite! Unlike true nettles, it's completely harmless and pleasant to touch. The name comes from its family relationships rather than any defensive properties.
compareHints: Unlike other hedgenettles in New England, woolly hedgenettle is the only one with thick, densely woolly leaves that feel soft to touch. Native hedgenettles like marsh woundwort have thin, green leaves that may be slightly hairy but never approach the plush, silvery-white texture of this species. The ornamental garden origin also sets it apart from our native Stachys species that prefer wetlands and wild areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hedge-nettle relatives, this species stands out for its narrow, hyssop-like leaves and preference for wetter habitats.
Marsh woundwort differs from its hedge-nettle cousins by its preference for consistently wet habitats rather than just moist woodland edges.
Among New England's hedge nettles, marsh hedge nettle stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, soft-textured leaves and stems compared to its smoother relatives.
Prairie woundwort differs from marsh woundwort by preferring dry rather than wet habitats and having broader, more heart-shaped leaves.
